prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are, in my judgement, the cleanest case on the shortlist of a measurement advance that has changed what can be observed. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening, and Ye's group converted that into systematic uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, including the many-body, spin-exchange regime. The evidence is the kind I trust: fractional uncertainty, Allan deviation and frequency ratios measured between independent clocks, and comparisons at the 1e-18 level from JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE. The downstream reach is real and already demonstrated: relativistic redshift over millimetre height differences, bounds on drifts of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, and the formal discussion of redefining the SI second. A two-person credit (proposal and realisation to the limit) is compact and defensible.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is territorial. Hall and Hansch were honoured in 2005 for the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable, and Wineland in 2012 for control of single ions that underlies the ion clocks; a sceptic can say the Nobel Prize has already paid for the enabling tools. There is also a genuine attribution tail: Lemonde, Peik, Ludlow, Bloom, Lemke, Hinkley and others shaped the clock, and the best ion clocks still compete on accuracy. Finally, humanity-level benefit is mostly prospective until the second is redefined or clock-based geodesy is routine.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranked B029 last on her list, questioning whether it is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and noting that the societal benefit is still largely prospective, and she put the NV-centre work (B001) first, crediting only Wrachtrup and Jelezko.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously but think it is answered by what was actually recognised. The 2005 citation was for the comb and comb-based precision spectroscopy, and 2012 was for measuring and manipulating individual quantum systems; neither covered trapping a many-atom ensemble at the magic wavelength to reach 1e-18 stability, which is a different physical route past the quantum-projection-noise limit of a single ion. On benefit, I would say the redefinition of the second and clock-network geodesy are concrete and near, not speculative. I agree that B001 is a real discovery and I ranked it fifth; where I differ is that the NV sensing record is still being established against competing sensors, whereas clock comparisons are already at the 1e-18 level. I also agree that restricting B001 to Wrachtrup and Jelezko would be the cleaner attribution if it comes up.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth, who also ranked B029 first, emphasises precision and robust theory-experiment agreement, regards the two-name credit as fair and compact, and flags that credit for the proposal history (Lemonde, Peik) and for comb and ion-clock pioneers is not fully settled.
responses.response: I agree on the core and on the two names, but I would not wave away the proposal-history point. Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength scheme is well documented, and the related lattice-clock ideas from other groups are largely contemporaneous refinements rather than the origin, so I am comfortable anchoring the citation on the magic-wavelength trapping concept. Where I would go further than her opening note is that the citation should be written around the measurement achievement (control of systematics to 1e-18) and not around the idea alone, because it is the realisation across several independent laboratories that makes this a prize-grade result.

responses.point: Goran Johansson ranked circuit QED (B004) first, arguing that strong coupling of a superconducting artificial atom to a microwave photon underpins virtually all superconducting processors and is a natural successor to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
responses.response: I ranked B004 second and agree that cQED is original, widely reproduced and enabling. My reservations are timing and attribution. The 2025 prize was for superconducting circuits, so even if the physics is distinct (light-matter coupling and dispersive readout versus macroscopic tunnelling), the Committee would be giving superconducting-circuit work two prizes in two years. On attribution, four credited names and a transmon contribution (Koch, Houck and colleagues) not in the list make a three-person set hard to defend; dropping Blais or Girvin is a real judgement call that the scientific record does not settle. I would therefore keep B004 as an alternative rather than the lead.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B031) first, as a theory prediction followed by a decisive experiment that opened a large field, and judged that recognition would not be premature even though the superconducting mechanism is debated.
responses.response: I accept that B031 is a striking discovery with a clean prediction-then-experiment structure, and that it has been reproduced by many groups. My hesitation is that Cao, Fatemi and others are outside the credited trio, that twist-angle disorder makes device-to-device reproducibility a real issue, and that the pairing mechanism is still open; for a field under ten years old I would be more comfortable once the interpretation has settled. By contrast, the lattice clock result has had a stable interpretation and cross-laboratory agreement for years. That is a question of maturity and not of scientific merit, and I would listen to Olle if he can argue that the physics is already settled enough.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee considers the 2005 and 2012 prizes to have covered enough of precision optical spectroscopy that a clock prize is no longer distinct.

Whether Katori's proposal and Ye's realisation should be weighted equally, and how to word the citation so that it covers the many-body clock without excluding ion-clock or other lattice-clock contributors.
Whether the Committee wants to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before awarding.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B029. I spent a year of my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is a 2005 laureate for the comb; Katori and Ye are not among my listed connections, but the Hall link and my general closeness to the laser-spectroscopy community should be noted. For B001 and B004, my own work on rare-earth crystals and quantum memories is in an adjacent area, and my WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Goran Johansson works, which is relevant if B004 is discussed.
